articles.title: What happened to Christa Pike? Tennessee death row inmate survives two lethal injections as governor halts executions
articles.summary: Christa Pike was scheduled to be executed in Tennessee on September 30, 2026, nearly 32 years after the murder that put her on death row.
articles.body: Christa Pike was scheduled to be executed in Tennessee on September 30, 2026, nearly 32 years after the murder that put her on death row. Instead, the execution ended with Pike being taken to hospital after surviving two injections of pentobarbital. She was reported to be in critical condition.The unusual case has now raised fresh questions about how Tennessee carries out lethal injections, what happened inside the execution chamber and what comes next for Pike.Why was Christa Pike on death row?Pike was 18 when she was involved in the 1995 killing of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a fellow Job Corps participant in Knoxville. Pike was convicted of murder and sentenced to death in 1996. Her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, was also convicted in the case and received life imprisonment plus 25 years.Pike remained on death row for decades while pursuing legal challenges. In September 2026, the US Supreme Court rejected her request to stay the execution.What went wrong during the execution?According to Pike's lawyers, officials struggled to establish an intravenous line before administering the drugs. After the first dose of pentobarbital, Pike was still alive, prompting officials to administer a second dose under Tennessee's protocol.The Tennessee Department of Correction said it followed the state's approved execution procedure and that the protocol did not permit additional procedures beyond those carried out. Pike was eventually transported to an outside medical facility.Her lawyers have described the episode as an unconstitutional use of lethal injection and are seeking to have her death sentence commuted. That request remains a legal matter rather than a settled outcome.What happens to Pike now?As of October 2, Pike remains alive and hospitalised. Her lawyer Randy Spivey said there was no clear prognosis yet. Her legal team is considering further options while asking Tennessee officials to commute her sentence.The state has not announced that Pike's death sentence has been changed. Her future will depend on legal and executive decisions that are still unfolding.Why has Tennessee paused executions?Governor Bill Lee ordered a third-party review of what happened and paused executions in Tennessee for the remainder of 2026. The decision also affects the scheduled December execution of Gary Wayne Sutton.The Pike case is also part of a wider debate about capital punishment and execution procedures. A US Bureau of Justice Statistics report records how execution methods have changed across states, while a National Institute of Justice review found that research has not established a reliable conclusion about whether the death penalty deters homicide.For now, the central unanswered question is simple: how did an execution designed to cause death leave the prisoner alive and critically ill? Tennessee's independent review is expected to examine exactly that.Disclaimer: This article is based on publicly available court records, Tennessee government statements and current news reports. Pike's medical condition and legal status may change as new information becomes available. The account of what occurred inside the execution chamber includes allegations from her lawyers that have not been independently established.Get the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates. articles.title: Lucky Bamboo: Best Placement for Money, Career and Family Luck This October
articles.summary: Lucky bamboo might be the easiest \"good luck\" plant you'll ever own.
articles.body: Lucky bamboo might be the easiest "good luck" plant you'll ever own. It barely needs soil, survives low light and costs less than a pumpkin spice latte at most grocery stores.But in feng shui, where you put it matters more than how pretty it looks. A stalk tucked behind the TV doesn't do much. The right corner, though? That can change how a room feels.Fun fact first. Lucky bamboo isn't actually bamboo. It's a type of dracaena. The feng shui meaning stays the same either way.Why October Is a Good Time to Add One2026 is the Year of the Fire Horse. Fire energy is fast and exciting, though it can leave homes feeling restless.Bamboo belongs to the wood element, which feeds steady growth. And the water it sits in adds calm. So a healthy lucky bamboo plant brings a little balance into a fiery year. With fall cleaning already underway in many homes, it's a natural time to bring one in.For Money: The Wealth CornerStand at your front door facing inside. The far left corner of your home, or of any single room, is known as the wealth area in Western feng shui.Place your lucky bamboo there. A home office desk works especially well, since that's where many people handle bills and budgets.If you follow the compass method instead, look for the southeast part of your home. Both approaches are common, so pick the one that makes sense to you.Choose a plant with five, six or eight stalks for wealth. Tie a red or gold ribbon around them. In Chinese tradition, both colours are linked with prosperity.For Career: Near the Entrance or Your DeskIn Western feng shui, the career area sits at the front centre of a home, near the main door. Compass-based feng shui puts it in the north.A small arrangement on an entry table helps "welcome" new opportunities. Working from home? Then set it on the left side of your desk, within your line of sight. Seeing something green and growing during a long workday does wonders for focus.Three stalks are a popular choice here, since the number is tied to happiness and good fortune.For Family: The Middle Left WallFamily harmony connects with the middle section of the left wall when you stand at the front door. The compass equivalent is east.The living room is ideal, since that's where the family gathers. A tall bamboo arrangement on a side table or bookshelf works well. Add family photos close by to strengthen the intention.Many people choose nine stalks for family luck, because nine stands for completeness and long life in Chinese tradition.Stalk Numbers to KnowTwo stalks represent love and partnership. Seven is often linked with health. Larger counts like 21 are sometimes gifted as powerful blessings for big milestones.But avoid four. In Chinese, the word for four sounds a lot like the word for death, so it's considered unlucky.Keep It HealthyA yellowing plant sends the opposite message of luck. So care matters.Use filtered or distilled water if your tap water is heavily treated, since chlorine and fluoride can brown the leaves. Change the water every week or two. Keep it out of harsh direct sunlight, which burns the leaves quickly.One more thing. Lucky bamboo is toxic to cats and dogs. If you have pets that like to chew plants, place it on a high shelf out of reach.Spots to SkipBathrooms drain energy in feng shui, so keep bamboo out of them unless it's purely decorative. Also avoid placing it right next to a trash can or in a dark, cluttered corner.And if a stalk dies, remove it promptly. Replace it so the total number still carries a good meaning.Get the latest astrology news and horoscope updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: From vehicle seizure to licence suspension: What happens if you don’t pay traffic challans?
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Ignoring traffic challans could soon mean more than just an unpaid fine.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Ignoring traffic challans could soon mean more than just an unpaid fine. The Supreme Court has directed states and Union territories to take stringent action against vehicles with pending e-challans, including impounding them and blocking several online services until the dues are cleared.A bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and K V Viswanathan said simply issuing e-challans was not enough, noting that nearly 47% of challans issued across the country remain unpaid.The court directed authorities to carry out random checks and impound vehicles if they are found to have outstanding e-challans.RC, fitness, PUC services may be blockedThe Supreme Court said online services for vehicles with unpaid traffic fines should be frozen. Authorities should bar renewal of registration certificates (RCs), issuance of duplicate RCs and requests to update the owner's address until pending fines are cleared.The court also directed authorities to deny fitness certificates to such vehicles and blacklist them on the Parivahan portal.The restrictions could also affect vehicle ownership transfers. The court said authorities should block the transfer of ownership of vehicles with outstanding challans, potentially preventing owners from selling them.Most significantly, the bench directed that no centre should be permitted to issue a pollution under control (PUC) certificate for vehicles with pending traffic fines.Driving licence action for multiple violationsThe Supreme Court also called for action against repeat offenders. For multiple traffic violations, authorities should stop renewal of the driving licence and take steps to suspend licences that are currently valid, the bench said.“Let there be random checking of vehicles, and if it is found that the e-challan issued has not been abided or honoured, necessary steps shall be taken to impound the vehicle itself,” the court said.Pulling up authorities for failing to recover pending fines, the bench said issuing lakhs of e-challans was not enough and questioned what was being done to actually recover the money.Rs 49,194 crore in challans pending recoveryThe court was informed that states and UTs have around Rs 49,194 crore to recover from e-challans issued over a period of time. Of this, around Rs 26,175 crore has been recovered, leaving a substantial amount still outstanding.The bench said authorities needed to work at the ground level and take into account the realities of enforcement.“We want to convey something to states/UTs/authorities in a plain and simple manner. It is not just sufficient to keep issuing e-challans to the person who is alleged to have violated the provisions of the law,” the court said.The case has been before the Supreme Court for nearly 14 years, after the writ petition was filed in 2012. The court said it had issued several directions over the years for effective implementation of the Motor Vehicles Act and Central Motor Vehicles Rules.It warned that if its directions continued to remain only on paper, the court could take “stern action” against the authorities.What can happen if traffic challans remain unpaid?Vehicle can be impounded during random checks.RC renewal can be blocked.Duplicate RC issuance can be stopped.Owner-address updates can be denied.Fitness certificate can be withheld.Vehicle can be blacklisted on Parivahan.Ownership transfer can be blocked, making it difficult to sell the vehicle.Driving licence renewal can be stopped in cases involving multiple violations.Existing driving licence can be suspended.PUC certificate can be denied.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) is set to hold a “Jail Bharo Andolan” against chief election commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar at Mumbai’s
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) is set to hold a “Jail Bharo Andolan” against chief election commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar at Mumbai’s Shivaji Park today, with founder Abhijeet Dipke making a fresh appeal to people to join the protest.In a new video, Dipke was seen posing with an auto driver as the two urged commuters and residents to gather at the protest venue. "Chala chala shivaji park.. shivaji park… shivaji park…," the caption reads.The auto driver in the video can be heard saying 'Shivaji Park 4 baje'.The CJP has announced a “Jail Bharo Andolan” against Kumar at Shivaji Park at 4pm, Gate No. 6, demanding Kumar’s resignation over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. Protest planned across citiesMassive protests are planned in Delhi and Mumbai today, with the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) set to launch its nationwide agitation from Mumbai’s Shivaji Park, the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), All India Students’ Association (AISA), National Students’ Union of India (NSUI) and Indian Youth Congress (IYC) have announced a separate demonstration at Jantar Mantar in Delhi.The CJP has said its agitation will be expanded to other parts of the country.“Appointment of CEC should be transparent; there should be involvement of civil society,” Dipke said in Mumbai.Police deny permission in Delhi, MumbaiPolice in both Delhi and Mumbai have denied permission for the proposed protests. In Delhi, prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) are in force across the New Delhi district, restricting public meetings or assemblies of five or more people, processions, demonstrations, picketing and dharnas without prior written permission.Delhi DCP said that the restrictions have been imposed to ensure public safety, maintain public order and facilitate smooth traffic movement.In Mumbai, police have also denied permission for the proposed gathering at Shivaji Park. Police said they were not authorised to permit such a gathering there in view of a 2013 Bombay High Court order and described the area as a silence zone.Meanwhile, multi-layer barricades have been put up on roads leading to Jantar Mantar, including Tolstoy Marg, Janpath Road and Sansad Marg. The Delhi Metro has also closed entry and exit at 11 stations, including Rajiv Chowk, Central Secretariat, Janpath, Patel Chowk, Seva Teerth, Mandi House, Lok Kalyan Marg, INA, Chawri Bazar, Ramakrishna Ashram Marg and New Delhi, until further notice.Why are protests being held against Gyanesh Kumar?The CJP and opposition parties have criticised Kumar over the SIR of electoral rolls and demanded his resignation.Their criticism intensified after it emerged that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had recorded objections on at least 14 occasions over 10 months to certain decisions and orders, some of which they said were issued without their knowledge.The Election Commission later clarified that the three-member commission had taken all decisions, including those relating to the SIR, unanimously.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: He never married or had children; after his death, his estate began funding engineering students at NC State, where he once studied
articles.summary: Guy Burke never married and had no children, but his legacy has continued to teach students at the university where he once struggled to afford his
articles.body: Guy Burke never married and had no children, but his legacy has continued to teach students at the university where he once struggled to afford his education. His connection with NC State began in 1953, when his interest in aircraft led him to study mechanical and aeronautical engineering. His path to graduation was interrupted several times after his father’s death forced him to leave college to earn money for tuition. Military service caused another break. Burke finally graduated in 1962 and spent three decades as a civilian employee of the US Navy. After his death in 2019, the estate gift he had arranged decades earlier became a scholarship supporting engineering students.Burke’s college journey took him from engineering classes to drafting workBurke grew up in Taylorsville, North Carolina, as the eldest of four siblings. His brothers remembered him as a capable student who also enjoyed baseball. In 1953, his interest in aeroplanes led him towards engineering at NC State.The early part of university life was relatively ordinary. He lived in Owen Hall, took part in ROTC, which was compulsory at the time, and worked through his engineering courses. But the subject was difficult for him. He was apparently more naturally comfortable with writing and drawing than some of the technical demands of the degree. Then, in May 1955, the family lost its father, Walton.The financial consequences changed Burke’s education. His mother could cover the family’s basic needs, but there was little left for university fees and living costs. Burke began moving in and out of college, working until he had saved enough to return.As reported by NC State University, at one point, he stayed at a relative’s hunting lodge and worked as a draftsman designing bridges for the state highway department. His university education became something he pursued between periods of employment rather than in one uninterrupted stretch.Burke returned to NC State after two years teaching soldiers at Fort SillBurke’s return to college did not mean his path was settled. In 1959, he was drafted into the US Army and spent two years at Fort Sill, Oklahoma, where he worked as an artillery instructor. He also played softball on the base. Teaching suited him, according to his family, and the experience became another part of a life in which education and work repeatedly overlapped.After completing his service, Burke returned to NC State. He finally finished his remaining courses in the summer of 1962. His brother David later described the experience as a story of determination to become an engineer at NC State.Three decades working for the US NavyBurke subsequently spent about 30 years as a civilian employee of the US Navy. His engineering background placed him in work connected with early military uses of GPS, at a time when the technology was still far removed from the consumer devices that would eventually make satellite navigation familiar to the public. Away from work, he had a strong interest in sport and collecting memorabilia. He held season tickets for the NFL's Washington Commanders and was a regular at games.Later in life, after retiring to Cary, North Carolina, Burke helped care for his sister Janice. He continued attending NC State sporting events and followed the Carolina Hurricanes. Burke was a careful investor and kept money in a range of mutual funds. His family described him as disciplined with his finances rather than someone who spent lavishly.Burke planned his NC State gift more than two decades before his deathBurke contacted NC State's College of Engineering in 1997 to ask about making a contribution. He did not immediately settle on what form that gift should take. After considering his options for several months, he decided to leave part of his estate to the university through his will.The choice of destination was closely connected to his own experience. He wanted the money to support engineering students, with scholarships taking both academic merit and financial need into account. That decision was made more than two decades before his death.Burke died on 22 March 2019, aged with no children to inherit the estate. His brother David, who served as executor, later worked with NC State's Office of Gift Planning to carry out the wishes set out in Burke's will. The resulting Burke Endowment began supporting students in 2020.Scholarships ease financial pressure for engineering studentsReportedly, for the 2025-26 academic year, 15 students from different class years received scholarships supported by the endowment. Some have worked throughout university to cover tuition and housing, while others have worried about taking on student debt or being able to study full-time.Angela Sarahi Hernandez, a member of the class of 2028, said, “The Burke Endowment has allowed me to attend NC State as a fulltime student rather than being a part-time student. Spending more time on campus has enabled me to focus on my academics and pursue undergraduate research.”For J. Blake Patterson, from the class of 2027 described, “The Burke Endowment has allowed me to pursue my degree without the burden of student loan debt, limiting my stress and making my NC State experience more enjoyable.”How a $500 act of support shaped the Burke family legacyAfter Walton Burke died, the local Lions Club, where his father had been a member, lent Guy $500 to help him remain in education. He could repay the money when he was able.When Guy eventually had enough money to settle the debt, the club did something unexpected. Rather than taking the repayment, members told him to give the money to his sister so that she could use it for her own education. The same arrangement was then extended to Gerald. That single $500 loan therefore helped three Burke siblings through school. Gerald eventually repaid the money to a club treasurer who no longer remembered the original loan and had no record of it.Burke’s legacy now supports students facing financial challengesGuy Burke's life did not follow the conventional pattern of leaving a family home, business or fortune to children. He was an unmarried man without children, remembered by his relatives for his engineering career, sporting interests, collecting and careful approach to money.His estate took on a different role. The provision he made in 1997 eventually became an endowment supporting students at the university where he had once struggled to pay for his own education. It has continued awarding scholarships each year since 2020.For his family, the connection between Burke's own circumstances and the students now receiving the money is difficult to miss. He knew what it meant to interrupt an education because of finances. He also knew what a modest helping hand could do, having benefited from the $500 loan given to his family.Decades after he first approached NC State about making a gift, the money he set aside is now being used by students working towards the same kind of qualification he once had to fight to complete.You use AI every day. articles.body: US Vice President JD Vance has called the H-1B visa programme “completely broken” and said he would support scrapping it, accusing companies of using the system to replace American workers with lower-paid foreign employees.In a video shared on X, Vance said the programme had been “totally taken advantage of” by technology companies, accounting firms and other businesses. He distinguished between hiring highly skilled foreign professionals and using H-1B visas to reduce labour costs.“If you’re going to bring in an accountant making $45,000 a year to replace an accountant who is an American making $60,000 a year, that’s not you using the programme to bring in a genius,” Vance said.“That’s you destroying American jobs and defrauding the American people,” he added.Vance defends $100,000 H-1B feeVance also defended the Trump administration’s controversial $100,000 payment requirement for certain H-1B petitions involving workers outside the US. The White House introduced the measure in September 2025 and extended it for another year in September 2026.Vance said the payment was intended to discourage companies from using the programme to hire cheaper foreign labour.“If you’re just trying to replace an American accountant with a cheaper foreign accountant, then you’re not going to pay $100,000,” he said.However, the fee is currently blocked following a federal court ruling. A second US district judge in California blocked enforcement of the $100,000 fee, finding that the administration had not followed the required rulemaking procedures.Vance’s remarks come as the Trump administration pursues broader changes to the H-1B system. A September 18 executive order directs the Departments of State, Labour and Homeland Security to consider whether an employer has recently laid off, or plans to lay off, similarly situated US workers while reviewing H-1B applications. It also directs the Labour Department to review previously filed labour-condition applications for possible violations.The administration has separately introduced a weighted H-1B selection system that gives greater weight to higher-paid positions.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2019, Jack Johnson's foundation bought neglected farmland in Hawaii; six years later, it reported over 40,000 pounds of produce harvested and more than 2,200 students welcomed on field trips
articles.summary: In 2019, musician Jack Johnson’s Kōkua Hawaiʻi Foundation acquired neglected farmland on Oʻahu with a plan to turn it into a place for education, food
articles.body: In 2019, musician Jack Johnson’s Kōkua Hawaiʻi Foundation acquired neglected farmland on Oʻahu with a plan to turn it into a place for education, food production and community involvement. Six years later, the Kōkua Learning Farm had reported harvesting more than 40,000 pounds of produce and welcoming over 2,200 students on educational field trips. The figures were included in a document submitted to the City and County of Honolulu, while the foundation’s Kōkua Learning Farm website describes the site’s wider work in farming, composting, agroforestry and food education. What began as a neglected agricultural property has gradually become a working classroom where children, teachers, volunteers and young farmers can learn how food is grown.From neglected land to a working farmThe Kōkua Learning Farm was created on land that had not been fully used for many years. Rather than treating the property simply as a place to grow crops, the foundation imagined a broader community resource that could connect people with Hawaiʻi’s food systems.The farm’s work reflects the Kōkua Hawaiʻi Foundation’s focus on environmental education and sustainable living. Its programmes encourage students to understand where food comes from, how soil is maintained and why healthy ecosystems are important to farms and communities.Turning neglected land into productive farmland required more than planting seeds. The property needed preparation, infrastructure, soil care and a long-term plan for managing water, crops, pathways and educational spaces. The gradual transformation allowed the organisation to build the farm around practical learning instead of creating a purely decorative garden.By the sixth year, the site had become a functioning agricultural operation. More than 40,000 pounds of produce had been harvested, showing how much food can emerge when land is restored with consistent care and community support.A place where students learn by doingOne of the farm’s most important roles is educational. More than 2,200 students had visited the property on field trips during the six years covered in the city document.The visits are designed to help students experience the food system directly. Instead of learning only from textbooks or classroom diagrams, children can see crops growing, examine soil, observe insects and discuss what happens to food scraps after meals.The foundation says field trips can include lessons on food production, compost, agroforestry and pollinators. Activities are adapted according to the age of the students, the size of the group and what is happening on the farm during the visit.That flexibility is important because farming is seasonal. A group visiting during planting will have a different experience from one arriving during harvest. Students may encounter seedlings, mature crops, composting projects, fruit trees or pollinator habitats, depending on the time of year.Hawaiian knowledge and ecological learningThe farm’s educational approach is also connected to Hawaiʻi’s relationship with the ʻāina, or land. The Kōkua Learning Farm website describes a Hawaiian Garden as the final piece of the farm’s development. The garden was designed through a collaborative process involving experts and community organisations.Such spaces can help students understand that agriculture is not only about producing food. It is also about caring for soil, water, plants, animals and the cultural knowledge connected to a place.The farm’s work includes agroforestry, a method that brings trees and crops together in a managed system. It also includes lessons about compost and pollinators, two parts of agriculture that are often overlooked when people focus only on the food found in markets.By bringing these subjects together, the farm gives visitors a more complete picture of how food is produced. A tomato or leafy green is not just the result of a seed and sunlight. It depends on soil health, water, pollinating insects, farm workers and careful management of the surrounding environment.Volunteers help keep the farm growingThe transformation of the property has also depended on public participation. The foundation hosts monthly community workdays, generally on the first Saturday of the month.Volunteers may help with mulching, weeding, collecting ʻōpala, or waste, working in the nursery, planting and harvesting. These tasks are ordinary parts of farm work, but they also give community members a direct role in maintaining the property.Private workdays are available for schools, businesses, churches, clubs, military groups and other organisations. These gatherings allow groups to work together outdoors while learning how much regular labour is needed to care for productive land.The farm also provides opportunities for individual volunteers during weekdays. This creates a connection between the property and the wider community, ensuring that the site is supported by more than a small staff.A training ground for young farmersThe Kōkua Learning Farm is not limited to younger children. It also runs a youth internship programme for students in grades nine through twelve.High school students from public schools, private schools and homeschool programmes can apply to become part of the cohort. Participants meet weekly and receive practical training as mahiʻai, or farmers.The programme covers agroecology, crop cultivation, fruit and vegetable production, soil health maintenance and culinary exploration. Students are able to see how farm decisions affect the food that eventually reaches a kitchen or table.The experience can also introduce young people to careers and forms of work they may not encounter in a conventional classroom. Farming, food education, environmental management and community organising all require scientific knowledge, physical effort and cooperation.More than a production siteThe 40,000 pounds of produce represent the farm’s visible output, but its impact is not limited to the weight of its harvest. The field trips, volunteer days, educator trainings and youth internships create a network of learning around the land.The foundation offers educator training connected to its ʻĀINA In Schools curriculum for kindergarten through sixth-grade students. These sessions give teachers hands-on opportunities to explore lessons that can later be used with students.That approach allows the farm’s influence to extend beyond visitors. A teacher who learns about composting, soil health or food production can take those ideas back to a school and introduce them to a much larger group of children.The site also hosts community events, farm workdays and farm-to-table activities. These programmes help connect food production with cooking, culture and shared community experiences.A long-term vision for the landSix years after the foundation acquired the neglected farmland, the Kōkua Learning Farm had become an example of what long-term restoration can achieve. The property was producing food, receiving school groups and giving volunteers a place to work with the land.Its progress also shows that restoring farmland is not an overnight project. The results depend on repeated tasks such as planting, harvesting, mulching, composting, repairing infrastructure and teaching visitors how the system works.Jack Johnson’s connection to the foundation has helped bring public attention to the project, but the farm’s development has relied on educators, farmers, students, volunteers and community partners. Their combined work has turned an underused property into a living classroom.For the children who visit, the most lasting lesson may be simple. Food does not begin on a supermarket shelf. It begins with land, water, seeds, people and the patient work of caring for all of them.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: ‘How many will you shut? People will come running’: CJP’s Saurav Das on 12 Delhi Metro station closures
articles.summary: MUMBAI: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) chief spokesperson Saurav Das on Friday reacted to the closure of entry and exit gates at 12 Delhi Metro stations amid
articles.body: MUMBAI: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) chief spokesperson Saurav Das on Friday reacted to the closure of entry and exit gates at 12 Delhi Metro stations amid security arrangements around Jantar Mantar, saying protesters would continue to reach the site despite the restrictions."How many metro stations will you shut down? People will come walking, and they'll come running too,” Das said in a post on X.In another post, Das said, “Gyanesh Kumar’s end will be the end of a tyrannical regime. The tyrant is deeply wounded. The people must prevail!”The Delhi Metro Rail Corporation has closed entry and exit gates at 12 stations until further notice, including Janpath, Patel Chowk, Central Secretariat, Rajiv Chowk, Seva Teerth, Mandi House, Lok Kalyan Marg, INA, Chawri Bazar, Ramakrishna Ashram Marg and New Delhi.Interchange facilities will remain available at Rajiv Chowk, Mandi House, New Delhi, Barakhamba and Central Secretariat.Police and Rapid Action Force (RAF) personnel and a riot control vehicle have been deployed at Jantar Mantar, while barricades have been put up on roads leading to the area. Additional security personnel have also been sought from the Union Ministry of Home Affairs in view of the expected turnout, police sources said.DCP New Delhi Sachin Sharma said Section 163 of the BNSS was in force in New Delhi and protests, demonstrations, marches and similar activities were not permitted.“Preventive arrangements have been made, and everyone is requested to follow the law and cooperate with the police,” Sharma said.He also advised people not to come to the area for protests or demonstrations, adding that necessary circulars, notifications and public awareness messages regarding roads and Metro services were being issued.Meanwhile, CJP has announced that it would begin a nationwide protest from Mumbai on Friday, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. articles.title: Egypt arrests entire editorial team of one of the country’s few independent media
articles.summary: Egyptian authorities swept up the entire editorial team of ‘Matsadaash’ one of the country’s few independent media, accusing them of belonging to the Muslim Brotherhood.
articles.body: NEW YORK — Egyptian authorities swept up the entire editorial team of one of the country’s few independent media, accusing them on Thursday of belonging to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood. The arrest this week of the six journalists of Matsadaash (Arabic for “Don’t Believe”) sparked an outcry from international and regional rights groups who called it an “alarming escalation on independent media and freedom of expression.” Authorities accused the six of being members of the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood, alleging they produced fabricated news for an online outlet in exchange for foreign funding. Matsadaash co-founder Abdelrahman Mansour denied the allegations and said he and their families have no idea where they are. “Everyone on this team knew the risks when they went to work every day, but it’s unacceptable for the government to make false accusations and forcibly disappear journalists just because they’re afraid of a free press,” he said, speaking from outside Egypt. “Their families are worried, we’re worried, we just want them released unharmed.” Founded eight years ago as a fact-checking platform, it has since expanded into investigative reporting in Egypt and other Arab countries. Mansour said two of the outlet’s editors were arrested in 2023 but were released without charge after State Security investigators found no affiliation with the Muslim Brotherhood. “It’s very difficult for us to understand why this is happening,” he said. Egypt is among the world’s worst jailers of journalists, according to the U.S.-based Committee to Protect Journalists. The Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights says 26 journalists are now behind bars in Egypt. The journalists’ whereabouts are unknown Egypt’s Interior Ministry on Thursday described Matsadaash as an unlicensed page managed from abroad by a “fugitive Brotherhood member,” it identified as Mansour. It said the six people detained were part of a Brotherhood “media committee” that prepared false and fabricated news for Mansour to publish. Only one of the six is a member of the Journalists’ Syndicate, the national press union, the statement said. It said legal measures have been taken but did not specify charges. The first arrest occurred on Monday night when authorities went to the home of Abdallah Qadry, Mansour said. The other five members of staff were arrested on Tuesday, starting with Mohamed Abu Emaira, who was taken from his home in the early hours. Mansour said Emaira’s library and internet router were destroyed during the arrest. Omar Helal was arrested in Port Said and Islam Barakat in Gharbia Governorate. Two other members of Matsadaash’s newsroom staff — Mohamed Mahmoud and Mohamed Adel — were arrested in Cairo. All had their cellphones and computers confiscated. The Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights said the whereabouts of all six remain unknown. “They have not been allowed to contact their families or legal team,” the advocacy group said. It was the first time an entire newsroom had been arrested in Egypt. Rights groups call for the journalists’ release Matsadaash, founded in 2018 as an online platform, has gained credibility and a large following in Egypt, where independent media are stifled and government censorship and oversight over newspapers and TV networks are the norm. The Matsadaash website is blocked in Egypt, but its Facebook page has more than one million followers. Over 80 international and regional rights groups, civil society organizations and independent media called on the Egyptian authorities to release the journalists, condemning what they called an escalating crackdown on independent media. “Matsadaash has operated openly for years and has built a reputation for credible and accurate reporting on a range of public interest issues across Egypt,” the petition, signed by groups including Human Rights Watch and Reporters Without Borders, said. “Egyptian authorities’ failure to allow free expression to thrive flies in the face of a purported commitment to dialogue, transparency, anti-corruption, and regional leadership.” Accusing critics of membership in the Brotherhood is common in Egypt, which designated the group as a terrorist organization in 2013, after the military ousted then-President Mohammed Morsi, a senior Brotherhood figure. Since then, authorities have frequently accused journalists and critics of belonging to the group or spreading false news. The Muslim Brotherhood, founded in 1928 in Egypt, began as a social and religious movement opposing British colonial rule. It grew into one of the Sunni Muslim world’s most influential Islamist movements, establishing branches in dozens of countries. Egyptian authorities alternated over the decades between tolerating and repressing the group, which was permitted to field candidates in elections for brief periods. The Muslim Brotherhood is now also banned in Jordan, while its branches are designated terrorist organizations by several countries.

articles.title: ‘They are crying’: Refugees in Malaysia in fear amid Myanmar deportation
articles.summary: Shrinking resources for refugee support groups in Malaysia collide with increasing hostility towards the Rohingya.
articles.body:
Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia – The phone hasn’t stopped ringing in recent days. Raf*, a leader of refugees from Myanmar who are living in Malaysia, receives more than 100 calls a day, and they follow a common pattern.

“They are crying, asking me to do something,” Raf told Al Jazeera.

The Malaysian government on Tuesday deported nearly 1,500 refugees, part of its stated plan to send back at least 5,000 refugees as part of a deal with the military government of Myanmar. That move, from a country that had long taken in the refugees, has sparked fear among the tens of thousands of other refugees from Myanmar in the country, who have one question at the top of their minds: Who might be next?

The deportation was carried out during escalating raids on refugee communities by immigration officials, which have led to the detention of more than 50,000 refugees this year alone. Those working with refugees in Malaysia said the frequency of the raids has increased since June when Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim announced the repatriation agreement with Myanmar.

“[We’ve seen] a sharp increase. Raids are happening every single day. There’s up to 50 raids or more happening every day,” said Heidy Quah, founder and executive director of the Malaysian nonprofit Refuge for the Refugees.

Minister of Home Affairs Saifuddin Nasution told local media that the government has conducted more than 9,700 such operations from the beginning of this year until September 17. That’s an average of 37 operations a day.

There are now more than 10,000 Myanmar nationals in Malaysia’s immigration depots, according to the Ministry of Home Affairs.

In all, Malaysia is home to more than 215,000 refugees, according to the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR). Nearly 194,000 are from Myanmar. There are more than 126,000 Rohingya refugees in Malaysia, where they have been the target of widespread hate speech on social media in recent months. Apart from the Rohingya, the Myanmar refugees in Malaysia include nearly 16,000 from the Chin community and 33,000 from other Myanmar communities. The non-Myanmar refugees in Malaysia include small numbers of Pakistanis, Yemenis, Somalis, Afghans, Syrians, Sri Lankans, Palestinians and Iraqis.

The Myanmar refugee community in Malaysia has yet to identify any Rohingya among the first nearly 1,500 people deported on Tuesday, community leaders told Al Jazeera. Instead, many are from Myanmar’s other ethnic minorities, who are more likely to have valid national identification documents, community leaders said.

“The Rohingyas are a problem for deportation because Myanmar denies their citizenship,” Raf said. “So I don’t think that Myanmar will agree and accept all those Rohingyas.”

Myanmar officially treats the Rohingya as Bangladeshi immigrants despite the community’s long roots in Myanmar and their distinct ethnic identity. The Myanmar army has repeatedly cracked down on the Rohingya minority, including a wave of violence in 2017 that many rights groups have described as genocide. It set off a major refugee crisis when hundreds of thousands of Rohingya fled to Bangladesh, Malaysia, India and other neighbouring nations.

Myanmar community leaders also said the raids this year appear to have targeted locations highlighted in anti-refugee videos on social media in which content creators filmed refugee-populated areas, portraying them as hubs of chaos. These videos have been shared thousands of times on platforms such as Threads, TikTok and Facebook.

Al Jazeera contacted the Immigration Department to verify the link between the videos and raids but had not received a response at the time of publication. Accounts that had posted and shared antirefugee sentiment also did not respond to requests for comment.

The increase in hostilities towards refugees in Malaysia coincides with a sharp decline in the capacity of local and international aid groups to support them, especially since the closure of the United States Agency for International Development in July 2025.

In Malaysia, this severely shrank resources for organisations helping refugees with basic needs, such as healthcare, Quah told Al Jazeera.

“Then slowly, United Nations organisations were being defunded, and even within the UN High Commissioner for Refugees in Malaysia, they lost a lot of staff,” Quah said. The job cuts reflected global retrenchments by UNHCR last year.

The agency continues to struggle with a funding crisis, saying on Tuesday that it faces a $5.79bn funding gap and, as of July, has received 32 percent of the funds it needs this year.

In Malaysia, this has led to even less protection for refugees and higher rates of exploitation, Quah said.

“Even UNHCR cardholders are arrested and remanded for about 14 days [while the] cards are verified,” she said.

For instance, an asylum-seeking woman who had scheduled an appointment to meet UNHCR representatives this month was recently detained, and immigration authorities demanded a letter from the organisation to prove that she was an asylum seeker, Quah said.

Although UNHCR confirmed the woman was seeking asylum, she remains in detention, Quah said.

UNHCR and rights groups in Malaysia have urged the Malaysian government to stop the deportations as violence continues in Myanmar.

A day before Malaysia’s deportation of the refugees on Tuesday, an air strike by Myanmar’s military was reported to have killed at least 33 people in Rakhine state, the historical home of the Rohingya. The Arakan Army group said the victims included vendors, shoppers and pedestrians. In June, the UN said Myanmar’s military was responsible for more than 700 civilian deaths over a six-month election period that started in August last year.

The Human Rights Commission of Malaysia (SUHAKAM) said that while Malaysia is not a party to the Refugee Convention of 1951, the principle of nonrefoulement has become part of customary international law and Malaysia, therefore, is bound to abide by it. The principle protects people from being returned to a place where they face a real risk of persecution, torture or other serious harm.

Particular attention should also be given to children, SUHAKAM said, highlighting that Tuesday’s deportation included 27 children, some reportedly as young as eight years old.

“No child should be returned to danger. Their safety, dignity and best interests must come first,” it said.

Myanmar community leaders in Malaysia told Al Jazeera the ships that departed on Tuesday will arrive in Yangon on Sunday.

“After that, we will [learn] whether they are allowed to leave the port safely [or are detained],” said one community leader who requested anonymity due to the increase in violence towards refugees in Malaysia.

Still, even those who are allowed to leave the port may need to spend months or years in Yangon because it is unsafe to travel across the country, the community leader said.

Rights groups further criticised the Malaysian government’s framing of the deportations as “voluntary”, saying individuals should have sufficient information about conditions in their home countries before making such a decision.

“While authorities say the returns are voluntary, those returned had been held in immigration detention. This raises serious questions about whether decisions to return were genuinely free and informed,” UNHCR Assistant High Commissioner for Protection Edem Wosornu said.

The Malaysian government said people were selected for deportation based on a list of names shared by the Myanmar government in an official diplomatic note.

“Such [a] ‘voluntary’ decision must be determined by an independent authority, such as the UNHCR, and not by the Immigration Department,” SUHAKAM said .

UNHCR told Al Jazeera that it was not involved in the latest return process and did not have access to the individuals concerned. “[We were,] therefore, not in a position to independently ascertain the voluntariness of their decisions to return,” it said.

“We continue to encourage the government to ensure that return processes include individual assessments, access to protection procedures and safeguards to ensure that any decision to return is free, informed and genuinely voluntary,” it said.

The deportations come at a time when Malaysia is simultaneously positioning itself as welcoming to refugees and their needs.

In 2015, the Malaysian government launched a Refugee Registration Document (DPP) programme. On paper, it is supposed to help register refugees, giving them official documentation.

Raf welcomed the DPP as long as the registration and documentation of refugees in Malaysia leads to access to work, education and healthcare.

“If these three things are provided, I think that’s a good solution for temporary refugees staying here.”

But the Malaysian branches of Amnesty International and Asylum Access said the latest deportations raise profound concerns about the purpose of the DPP. The programme should not be used to fast-track unlawful deportations, the groups said in a joint statement.

*Name changed to protect the individual’s identity

articles.title: Arab party leader forced to withdraw from Israeli elections
articles.summary: Palestinian participation in upcoming Knesset vote continues to shrink with withdrawal of Sami Abu Shehadeh.
articles.body:
Arab Israeli politician Sami Abu Shehadeh has withdrawn his candidacy for the upcoming Israeli elections after the Supreme Court advised him to drop out.

The leader of the left-wing Palestinian Balad party announced on Friday he was dropping his bid for election to the Knesset on October 27. His withdrawal, which came after the court threatened to disqualify him, comes amid increased efforts by Israeli authorities to block Arab Israeli parties from taking part.

Political analysts view Arab Israeli parties as potential kingmakers in the election, with polls showing neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition nor the main opposition bloc on course for an outright majority.

The withdrawal came after the Supreme Court indicated that a majority of its judges agreed with a September 23 decision from Israel’s Central Elections Committee to oust him from the race after nationalist political rivals accused him of supporting Hamas’s attack on October 7, 2023.

Adalah, a rights organisation representing Abu Shehadeh, condemned the court, saying the evidence it presented had no legal basis.

“The court has effectively decided to remove a Palestinian leader, a citizen of Israel, from the Knesset,” Adalah said in a statement.

“The court’s clear intention to disqualify him,” it added, was “a direction that would have set a dangerous legal precedent with devastating consequences.”

Abu Shehadeh served in the Knesset from 2019 to 2022. Balad confirmed he was withdrawing his candidacy but stressed that the decision did not mark the end of his political struggle and that he would remain party leader.

The elections committee voted to disqualify him at the request of far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, who accused him of supporting the Hamas attack due to an article issued the following day in which Abu Shehadeh called it an “important historical event”.

Speaking to the Supreme Court on Thursday, Abu Shehadeh said he did not support “armed struggle” but acknowledged that a paragraph in the article had been incorrectly worded. He said his intention was to call for moving the conflict towards a political process.

Adalah labelled his withdrawal from the election “a severe blow to the right of Palestinian citizens to be represented and to stand for election”.

The elections committee has also barred two Arab electoral lists: the United Arab List and the Joint List, a three-party alliance that includes Abu Shehadeh’s party Balad. The Supreme Court is due to continue hearing appeals from the parties on Friday.

Adalah has questioned why the Palestinian candidates are being disqualified but far-right Israeli candidates were “cleared to run” despite openly calling for violence against Palestinians and making statements “amounting to incitement to genocide”.

articles.title: British paratrooper killed by explosion in Ukraine, coroner rules
articles.summary: L/Cpl George Hooley is the first UK service member to die in Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.
articles.body:
A British paratrooper was killed by an explosion while assisting Ukrainian troops in the war with Russia, a coroner has ruled.

An inquest, conducted partly in secret this week, into L/Cpl George Hooley's death found he had "sustained multiple injuries from an explosion" on 6 December 2025.

Hooley, 28, died from his injuries in a hospital in Kyiv three days later - the first British service member to die in Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

Darren Salter, senior coroner for Oxfordshire, said he had been provided with "limited evidence" about the circumstances and cause of the explosion but Hooley's death was "not suspicious".

The location of the explosion is also unknown, other than that it was away from the front line.

The coroner's report said Hooley had been transferred from at least one other hospital in Ukraine before his death in the capital.

In a statement in December, the Ministry of Defence (MoD) said Hooley was "an exceptional soldier and an impressive junior leader with extensive operational experience".

It said his death was a "tragic accident" that happened while he was "observing Ukrainian forces test a new defensive capability".

The MoD did not comment when asked further questions about the circumstances of the incident.

Hooley's company commander in the Parachute Regiment said the 28-year-old was "a born soldier" who "had a rare gift: a deep kindness and genuine time for everyone".

Hooley, from Wallingford in Oxfordshire, joined the regiment in June 2016 after completing his training at the Infantry Training Centre Catterick in North Yorkshire.

The UK government has never disclosed the number of service people in Ukraine, but has previously acknowledged a small number is there to support Ukrainian armed forces and provide security to diplomatic personnel.

After almost five years of war, the front line in Ukraine remains largely stagnant with both sides failing to make significant gains.

Russia currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory, including a large area of Donetsk.

Peace negotiations to bring an end to the war have also stalled. Kyiv and its European allies accuse President Vladimir Putin of repeatedly rejecting plans for trilateral talks involving Russia the US and Ukraine and say he is seeking to seize more Ukrainian territory.

articles.title: Trump’s Iran crackdown collides with NATO ally seeking access to America’s prized fighter jet
articles.summary: U.S.-sanctioned Iranian airlines made at least 83 flights into Turkey after a key Treasury deadline, the Foundation for Defense of Democracies says.
articles.body: At least 83 flights operated by U.S.-sanctioned Iranian airlines landed in Turkey in the five days after a key American sanctions deadline, according to flight data analyzed by the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, putting a new spotlight on whether Washington will enforce its escalating pressure campaign against companies servicing the carriers in a NATO ally. The Sept. 28 FDD report said U.S. pressure has helped push Iranian airlines out of several regional markets, including Iraq, the United Arab Emirates and Oman, but found that Turkey remains a significant gap in Washington’s effort to ground the carriers. The findings come after the Treasury Department announced sweeping new sanctions on Iran’s aviation industry on Sept. 8, designating all 27 remaining active Iranian airlines under Executive Order 13902. Treasury said Iran's aviation sector has been used to transport weapons, personnel and illicit cargo and warned foreign businesses about the risks of continuing to support sanctioned carriers. TRUMP PUSHES F-35 SALE TO TURKEY, BUT HIS OWN STATE DEPARTMENT SAYS ERDOĞAN HASN'T MET LEGAL REQUIREMENTS The continued Iranian flights come at a sensitive moment in U.S.-Turkey relations. Turkey is a NATO ally, and President Donald Trump has publicly emphasized his close relationship with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan while signaling openness to restoring Ankara’s access to the F-35 fighter jet program. Turkey was removed from the program after purchasing Russia’s S-400 air-defense system, a move that also triggered U.S. sanctions in 2020. During a July 2026 visit to Turkey, Trump said his administration would lift those sanctions and was considering allowing Ankara to buy F-35s, though congressional restrictions tied to Turkey’s possession of the S-400 remain an obstacle. Erdoğan said as recently as Sept. 24 that he expects Washington to take "concrete steps" toward Turkey’s return to the program. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that after a Sept. 23 wind-down deadline, companies providing sanctioned Iranian airlines with services such as fuel or landing support risked losing access to the U.S. financial system. FDD cited Bessent saying that by that date, Iranian airlines would be "shut down around the world." But FDD researchers Ahmad Sharawi and Sinan Ciddi said their review of Flightradar24 flight histories showed that at least 83 flights operated by U.S.-sanctioned Iranian carriers landed in Turkey between Sept. 23 and Sept. 27, after that deadline had passed. The flights landed in Istanbul, Ankara and Izmir, according to the report. The researchers identified 12 sanctioned Iranian airlines among the arrivals. Iran Airtour and Caspian Airlines each accounted for 12 landings, Iran Air for 10, and ATA Airlines and AVA Airlines for nine each, according to FDD. Eight of the 12 carriers identified in the flight data were among the airlines newly designated by Treasury on Sept. 8. IRAN LOSES KEY ECONOMIC LIFELINE IN MIDDLE EAST THAT TRUMP'S SANCTIONS COULDN'T REACH AS DEADLOCK PERSISTS The Treasury Department told Fox News Digital that it has continued raising the issue directly with senior Turkish officials and has warned Turkish companies and financial institutions about their potential sanctions exposure. "Following Treasury’s productive engagements with senior Turkish authorities last month, which quickly translated into tangible results — including the cancellation of Mahan Air flights and the revocation of Bank Mellat’s license — we have continued discussions regarding Türkiye’s aviation links to Iran and the sanctions exposure Turkish financial institutions and businesses face for facilitating these flights," a Treasury spokesperson told Fox News Digital. "We have made those risks clear and continue to address these issues at senior levels with the Turkish government," the spokesperson said. The Treasury spokesperson pointed to the administration’s broader "Operation Economic Outcast" campaign, saying it was producing results as Washington seeks to cut off Iran’s remaining sources of revenue and access to international markets. "Operation Economic Outcast is delivering results as Treasury and our partners continue to sever the Iranian regime’s remaining economic lifelines," the spokesperson said. "Iran’s rial has fallen to record lows, Iran loaded no crude oil onto tankers in September, and countries across the region are taking concrete steps to restrict Iran’s access to the international financial system and commercial aviation." "We will continue applying pressure and holding accountable those who provide the regime with the financial and commercial lifelines it needs to sustain its terrorist activities," the spokesperson added. Turkey has indeed taken some steps to limit aviation ties with Iran. Turkish Airlines, AJet and Pegasus removed flights to Iran from their schedules, while Mahan Air suspended service to Turkey beginning Sept. 21, according to Turkish Minute, citing airline schedules and reporting by the Financial Times and other outlets. Mahan Air has been under U.S. sanctions since 2011. The Treasury Department said at the time that the airline provided financial, material and technological support to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps-Quds Force. Other sanctioned Iranian airlines, however, have continued flying into Turkey. Caspian Airlines and Meraj Air were designated by Treasury as Specially Designated Global Terrorists in August 2014. Treasury said Caspian had transported IRGC personnel and weapons to Syria and said Meraj had ferried illicit cargo, including weapons, to the Syrian government. Sharawi told Fox News Digital that the continued flights reflect a gap between Ankara’s public steps and its handling of sanctioned Iranian carriers. "The fact that sanctioned Iranian airlines continue to land in Turkey, despite Washington’s clear effort to restrict their operations, is a testament to Ankara’s willingness to take symbolic measures while turning a blind eye to much of Iran’s broader activity," Sharawi said. MILLIONS OF BARRELS OF IRANIAN OIL SIT BEYOND TRUMP BLOCKADE AS HE VOWS ‘ZERO LEAKAGE’ Sharawi argued that Washington could increase pressure by targeting Turkish companies that continue providing services to sanctioned Iranian carriers. "Ankara may think it can get away with this, but Washington has not hesitated in the past to sanction Turkish entities that support sanctioned Iranian actors," he told Fox News Digital. "Continuing to target companies that provide that support would send a clear message to Ankara that facilitating Iran’s sanctioned networks will carry consequences." He said such measures could have a practical effect on Iran’s ability to maintain the routes. "If the United States targets the support system that keeps these sanctioned Iranian carriers operating, private Turkish companies will have much less incentive to continue doing business with them," Sharawi said. "If those companies begin cutting ties, it could significantly restrict Iranian airlines’ ability to operate routes to Turkey." The Turkey findings come as another advocacy group is raising concerns about a different potential weak point in Washington’s campaign to isolate Tehran: Iranian maritime commerce in waters near Malaysia. United Against Nuclear Iran said Sept. 25 that its investigators traveled roughly 100 nautical miles into the South China Sea near Malaysia’s Eastern Outer Port Limits, where the group said it observed Iranian-linked tankers, cargo vessels and bulk carriers alongside Malaysian bunker vessels supplying ships with fuel. UANI described the concentration of ships as a "floating city" supporting Iran’s sanctions-evasion network. Those findings were produced by UANI and have not been independently verified for this draft. EXCLUSIVE: RUSSIAN DOCUMENT REVEALS SWEEPING IRAN PLAN SPANNING NUCLEAR, FINANCE AND AVIATION "After seeing this floating city of ghost tankers with our own eyes, it is clear it is serving as an illicit Malaysia-backed lifeline for the Iranian regime," UANI CEO Ambassador Mark D. Wallace said in a Sept. 25 statement. He accused Malaysian entities of providing support that allows Tehran to continue generating revenue despite international efforts to economically isolate the regime. Former Florida Gov. and UANI Chairman Jeb Bush and Wallace called on the Treasury Department to sanction entities associated with Malaysia’s Pengerang petroleum complex as well as Malaysian entities or officials they allege are facilitating the trade. Their call for sanctions is an advocacy position and does not establish that the Malaysian entities have violated U.S. law. Fox News Digital has learned that Treasury has mapped Iranian oil-smuggling networks, facilitators and financial channels, including deceptive shipping activity off the coast of Malaysia, and that senior Treasury officials continue to raise the issue with Malaysian and other foreign government counterparts. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Taken together, the findings from FDD and UANI highlight what the organizations describe as continuing enforcement challenges as Washington attempts to cut Iran off from international aviation, shipping and financial networks. Treasury has continued expanding that campaign: on Sept. 29, it announced another round of sanctions targeting individuals and companies it said had procured weapons and components for Iran’s Ministry of Defense and Armed Forces Logistics. articles.title: Flávio Bolsonaro inherited his father’s right-wing movement. Can he win Brazil’s presidency?
articles.summary: Flávio faces a task that even his father could not accomplish: defeating Brazil’s leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who, at nearly 80, is seeking a fourth and likely final term.
articles.body: Standing atop a truck equipped with loudspeakers on Rio de Janeiro’s Copacabana Beach, Brazilian senator Flávio Bolsonaro officially launched his campaign, addressing the inevitable comparison with the man whose footsteps he is trying to follow. “I know you are looking at me right now and thinking of someone,” he told thousands of supporters gathered on August 16 in the city where his political career began. “I know I look like him, but it is difficult to compare Pelé’s son to Pelé.” The reference to Brazil’s most famous soccer player drew laughter, but it captured the challenge at the heart of Bolsonaro’s presidential candidacy: how to capitalize on his similarities with his father, ex-President Jair Bolsonaro, while convincing voters that a different Bolsonaro can inherit the movement built around him. The physical resemblance is obvious. Flávio shares his father’s light-colored eyes, dark hair, defined features and some of his gestures when speaking. But as he campaigns to succeed the man who transformed Brazil’s right, he has struggled to connect with voters in the same way his father did. That is why, for much of the rally, escaping Jair Bolsonaro’s shadow did not even seem to be the goal. Flávio played recordings of the former president, promised to continue his legacy and said he had “humbly” accepted the mission his father had entrusted to him. Convicted of more than 27 years in prison for plotting a coup after his 2022 electoral defeat, Jair Bolsonaro has entrusted Flávio with continuing his legacy, while maintaining his innocence and hoping that his son’s path to the presidential palace could also lead to his own freedom. At 45, Flávio now faces a task that even his father could not accomplish: defeating Brazil’s leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who, at nearly 81, is seeking a fourth and likely final term. But just days before the first round, both candidates face controversies — corruption allegations, family disputes and a growing institutional crisis involving the Supreme Federal Court and figures across the establishment — while polls show an increasingly close race. A more moderate Bolsonaro? Flávio Nantes Bolsonaro was born in 1981 and is the eldest of Jair Bolsonaro’s five children. A lawyer by profession, he was elected to the Rio de Janeiro state legislature at just 21, long before his father’s rise turned the family name into one of Brazil’s most powerful political brands. Flávio served four terms before reaching the Senate in 2018, the same election in which his father won the presidency. He built his political career in Rio de Janeiro — a state with a long history of organized crime and violence — focusing primarily on hard-line public security policies and defending police officers and other security forces. However, Flávio is perceived as a more moderate and conciliatory Bolsonaro. “During the various crises of Jair Bolsonaro’s government, Flávio appeared to be the family member with some willingness to engage in dialogue,” said Octávio Amorim Neto, a political scientist and professor at the Getulio Vargas Foundation. During his father’s repeated clashes with Congress and the Supreme Federal Court, Flávio cultivated relationships with lawmakers and acted as an informal bridge between his father and the Senate. “Flávio has more tact than his father,” said Gilson Machado, Jair Bolsonaro’s former tourism minister, who has known the former president since the 1990s and Flávio for more than a decade. “He listens more.” Machado, a longtime Bolsonaro ally, was arrested on June 13, 2025 as part of an investigation into whether he had attempted to help Bolsonaro’s former chief of staff and a key witness in the coup-plot case obtain a Portuguese passport and leave Brazil. Machado denied the allegations, and his pretrial detention was revoked that same day, although he still faces restrictions, including the retention of his passport. Machado says he often spends vacations with Flávio in northeastern Brazil and that the senator loves fishing and is passionate about diving. “He is a fearless diver. He goes down to 30 meters (90 feet). I had never seen anything like it,” he said. Machado also offered a glimpse into one of the main differences between father and son: Jair’s more reserved nature compared with Flávio’s more openly affectionate personality. “Bolsonaro has never kissed his children,” he said. “Flávio, on the other hand, kisses his son; he has kissed his father. It is a different style.” But a more moderate personal style does not amount to a more moderate political project. In a 2007 speech, Flávio defended the militias that were expanding their control over parts of Rio at the time, describing them as a “new way of doing police work” that could provide security where the state had failed, in what is widely regarded as one of the most controversial episodes of his career. “As a state lawmaker, he awarded medals to militia members,” Amorim Neto said. “That is one of the major stains on his record, even in the eyes of the right.” A hard-line approach to crime is also a central element of his father’s movement, and Flávio has taken it to the national stage. His campaign puts security front and center, with promises to lower the age of criminal responsibility and toughen the response to violent crime. In March, he called for Brazil’s two largest criminal groups to be designated as terrorist organizations and then traveled to the United States in May to make the request directly to Trump, a measure rejected by Lula and the left, who consider it a threat to Brazilian sovereignty. When the United States announced that the groups would be designated as terrorist organizations, Bolsonaro thanked Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio for what he described as a response to his request. The message connects with voters’ main concern: A Quaest poll in August showed that 33% of Brazilians considered violence the country’s main problem, more than twice the percentage who mentioned the economy. A family business After Jair’s conviction left him out of the race, other prominent names emerged to take over the leadership of the right. But the former president pushed to keep the legacy within his own surname. “Politics is the Bolsonaro family business,” Amorim Neto said, and two of the brothers with the longest political careers thus emerged as the leading contenders. Eduardo Bolsonaro had built the strongest international profile among the brothers, cultivating ties with the MAGA movement in the United States and lobbying the Trump administration to pressure Brazil’s Supreme Federal Court over his father’s case. In July 2025, Trump called the case against Jair Bolsonaro a “witch hunt” and announced 50% tariffs on Brazilian imports. Nearly a year later, Brazil’s courts convicted Eduardo of coercion and sentenced him to four years and two months in prison. He remains in the US and risks being arrested if he returns to Brazil. “That effectively left Flávio and his stepmother, former first lady Michelle Bolsonaro, as the leading contenders to inherit the family’s political leadership,” Amorim Neto said. For the political scientist, Jair Bolsonaro’s final decision was to favor his own bloodline. “He ended up choosing the eldest son,” he said. But the transition was not easy. Flávio publicly clashed with his stepmother, the former first lady, a powerful figure on Brazil’s right. A dispute over party alliances erupted publicly in June, when Michelle posted videos accusing her stepson of humiliating her politically during a phone call. The rift was particularly delicate because Michelle had built a strong network among conservative women and evangelical Christians, key constituencies for Flávio. Flávio apologized, and the two publicly reconciled in July after weeks of efforts by party leaders to contain the dispute. By September, Michelle had returned to the campaign to support her stepson, asking her network of female supporters to help elect him. Machado told CNN that their relationship is now “as good as it can possibly be.” But the episode exposed a fragmented right and a divided Liberal Party, Bolsonaro’s political base. A scandal that reaches everyone The campaign is also facing other problems. A sweeping corruption investigation into the bankrupt private Brazilian bank, Banco Master, has become a backdrop to the election, reaching politicians across Brazil’s establishment, including the Supreme Federal Court, Lula and Flávio himself. For Flávio, the scandal initially presented an opportunity to revive one of Bolsonarismo’s longest-running battles: its confrontation with the Supreme Federal Court, and particularly with Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who oversaw key investigations that ultimately led to Jair Bolsonaro’s conviction. Bolsonaro supporters have since portrayed Moraes as an ally of Lula, although he was not appointed by Lula and does not belong to his party. Investigators uncovered a multimillion-dollar contract between Banco Master and a law firm owned by Moraes’ wife, as well as compromising messages that the bank’s president sent to a contact he had saved under Moraes’ name, according to CNN Brasil. It has not been established that Moraes received or responded to the messages, but the revelations gave Bolsonaro’s campaign enough ammunition to return to one of its most familiar arguments: that the left, and anyone associated with it, is corrupt. “Today we have our No. 10 on the campaign trail,” Machado told CNN. “It is Alexandre de Moraes.” CNN has reached out to Moraes for comment. He has previously denied receiving messages attributed to him, calling the association of his name with them a “false inference” aimed at attacking the Supreme Court. Luciano Da Ros, a political scientist specializing in corruption and Brazil’s judicial system, said that for the Bolsonaro base, interest in Moraes’ possible involvement goes beyond the election. “They hope this will eventually make it possible to overturn the conviction or invalidate his actions in the case on procedural grounds,” he said. But in recent days, the scandal has also reached Flávio. The Supreme Federal Court opened an investigation in July into the senator over alleged corruption and money laundering linked to Banco Master’s financing of “Dark Horse,” a film about Jair Bolsonaro. Flávio has denied wrongdoing and said his ties to Daniel Vorcaro, the former owner of Banco Master, were related to the film. Bolsonaro beyond Jair If elected, clashes with the judiciary are unlikely to end. Flávio has promised to seek a broad amnesty for his father and others convicted over the coup attempt, and to use the presidential pardon power if Congress does not act. “That would mean another enormous crisis with the Supreme Federal Court,” Amorim Neto said. A Flávio government is also expected to maintain much of his father’s international alignment, particularly with the US. “Bolsonarismo is intimately linked to MAGA and Trumpism,” Amorim Neto said, arguing that the Bolsonaro family has positioned itself as a follower of Trump’s political movement. But that closeness to Trump has also exposed a contradiction in Bolsonarismo’s nationalist message. “If you are a nationalist or a patriot, first and foremost you put the national interest ahead, not subordination to the leader of the world’s superpower,” Amorim Neto said. “And Brazilian voters see it, they perceive it, and most of them are against it, although Bolsonaro supporters among the electorate back several of Trump’s actions.” That contradiction has emerged repeatedly: in Trump’s tariffs on Brazilian products over the judicial proceedings against Jair Bolsonaro, which Eduardo Bolsonaro had lobbied for; in Flávio’s push for the US to designate Brazil’s largest criminal groups as terrorist organizations; and in debates over US interest in the country’s critical mineral resources. That marks a clear difference between Bolsonaro and Lula: While Flávio has aligned himself with Trump and a growing network of conservative leaders in Latin America, Lula has emphasized Brazil’s sovereignty and interests while deepening ties with China. Putting the power of a legacy to the test Still, those contradictions have not prevented Flávio from consolidating much of the loyal electorate that backed his father. Brazil remains deeply polarized, and the political distribution has changed little since 2022: Flávio draws some of his strongest support from evangelical Christians and higher-income voters, while Lula remains stronger among lower-income Brazilians and Catholics. In a Datafolha poll published in September, Flávio led Lula by nearly two to one among evangelical voters, while Lula maintained a smaller lead among Catholics, 43% to 32%. His emphasis on fighting crime, his anti-left agenda and his confrontations with the Supreme Federal Court and Brazil’s political establishment directly appeal to issues that have mobilized Bolsonaro’s base for years. According to a Quaest poll published in September, nearly all voters who identify as Bolsonaro supporters now back Flávio, suggesting that the movement’s political identity has been transferred even without its founder on the ballot. That inherited support has helped transform a candidacy that initially struggled to escape a turbulent campaign and the shadow of his father into a highly competitive race with Lula. At his first campaign rally in Copacabana, Flávio promised to continue his father’s legacy. And while he may not be a carbon copy of his father, that could be enough to win this October.
